Pool of Siloam
pool uv sy-LOH-um
proper noun (place)
From Hebrew Shiloach ("sent"), Greek Silōam; a pool in Jerusalem fed by the waters of the Gihon spring through Hezekiah's tunnel. John notes its name means "Sent" (John 9:7).

Biblical Definition

The Pool of Siloam was a pool in Jerusalem, at the southern end of the City of David, fed by the Gihon spring through the tunnel King Hezekiah had cut through the rock (2 Kings 20:20); it is chiefly famous as the place where the Lord Jesus sent the man born blind to wash and receive his sight. In John 9, the Lord encountered a man blind from birth; rejecting the disciples' assumption that the blindness was punishment for someone's specific sin, He declared that it was "that the works of God should be made manifest in him" (John 9:3). He spat on the ground, made clay, anointed the blind man's eyes, and said, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam (which is by interpretation, Sent). He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing" (John 9:7). The healing led to one of the great chapters of confrontation in the Gospels: the healed man, interrogated by the Pharisees who refused to believe, grew bolder in his testimony until he confounded them — "Whereas I was blind, now I see" (John 9:25) — and was cast out of the synagogue, whereupon the Lord found him and revealed Himself as the Son of God, and the man worshipped Him. John's parenthetical note that "Siloam" means "Sent" is theologically pointed: the Lord Jesus is the Sent One, the one whom the Father sent (a theme throughout John's Gospel), so that the blind man washing in the pool called "Sent" pictures the cleansing and illumination that come through the Sent One, Christ Himself. The water of Siloam (also associated, in the Feast of Tabernacles, with the water-pouring ceremony at which the Lord cried, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink," John 7:37) and the giving of sight to the blind together testify to Christ as the light of the world (John 9:5) and the giver of living water. The Pool of Siloam stands as a place where physical blindness was healed to display the deeper truth: that Christ the Sent One opens the eyes of the spiritually blind, and that those who come to Him, blind and helpless, go away seeing.

POOL OF SILOAM, proper noun. Hebrew Shiloach ("sent"); Greek Silōam; a pool in Jerusalem fed by the Gihon spring through Hezekiah's tunnel.

Where the Lord Jesus sent the man born blind to wash and receive his sight (John 9:1-7).

"Go, wash in the pool of Siloam (which is by interpretation, Sent)... and came seeing" (John 9:7).

The healing led to the man's bold testimony, his casting out of the synagogue, and the Lord's self-revelation (John 9).

John's note that Siloam means "Sent" points to Christ the Sent One, who opens the eyes of the spiritually blind (John 9:5).

Key Scripture

John 9:6-7 — "When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay, And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing."

John 9:25 — "He answered and said, Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see."

John 9:5 — "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world."

John 7:37 — "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink."

Modern Corruption

The Pool of Siloam is corrupted when the healing is read as mere miracle without its meaning, when the name "Sent" is missed as pointing to Christ, or when the spiritual blindness the chapter exposes (in the seeing Pharisees) is overlooked.

expand to see more

Name-meaning missed. John deliberately pauses to translate the name: the pool of Siloam means "Sent." This is no idle etymology. Throughout John's Gospel, the Lord Jesus is the Sent One, the one the Father sent into the world (John 3:17; 5:36-37; 17:18). The blind man washing in the pool named "Sent" to receive his sight is a living parable: cleansing and illumination come through the Sent One, Christ Himself. The man's physical sight, given through washing in "Sent," pictures the spiritual sight given to all who come to the Sent Savior. John's translation invites the reader to see the deeper meaning the water and the name carry.

The Pool of Siloam has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the contrast the chapter draws between the blind man who came to see and the seeing Pharisees who remained blind. The man born blind received both physical and spiritual sight, growing bolder in his confession until he worshipped Christ. The Pharisees, who had physical sight and religious learning, refused to see, and the Lord pronounced over them: "For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind... If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth" (John 9:39-41). The Pool of Siloam exposes the deeper blindness: the willful blindness of those who, claiming to see, reject the light of the world. The remedy for both blindnesses is the same — to come to Christ the Sent One, who gives sight to the blind and humbles the proud who think they see.
